They also congratulated Brunei Darussalam on the designation of its new National Influenza Centre, demonstrating that the network is continuing to grow and strengthen. “Our strength is in our network - in sharing expertise, information and capacities, and in supporting one another to be better prepared for the threats ahead,” said Dr Nilesh Buddha, Officer in Charge for the WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia. “Where expertise exists in one country, we should facilitate its transfer and application across the region; where specialized capacities are available, we should strengthen pathways for countries to access them.” Dr Buddha also stressed the importance of coordinated investments, resource mobilization and strategic prioritization at a time when resources are increasingly constrained. He called for greater collaboration to make optimal use of existing capacities, maximize impact and avoid duplication. In her closing remarks at the meeting, Dr Gina Samaan, the WHO Regional Emergency Director for the Western Pacific, called on participants to carry the ideas, contacts and tools discussed over the three days back to their national teams, and to continue working in solidarity on the timely sharing of influenza viruses and data, accurate virus characterization, and strengthened genomic sequencing capacity. She assured participants that WHO would continue to offer technical guidance and capacity-building support to Member States. “Surveillance data only matter when they change what public health systems do,” she said. “Information that sits in a spreadsheet protect no one, while information that reaches a decision-maker at the right moment saves lives.” The 19th Biregional Meeting of National Influenza Centres and Influenza Surveillance reaffirmed that as influenza A(H5N1) continues to test animal and human health systems, the strength of this surveillance network - and the countries and institutions that sustain it - remains one of the region’s most important lines of defence. ____________________ For more information, please contact: WHO South-East Asia Communications, SEMediaRelations@who.int WHO Western Pacific Communications, wprocom@who.int Fact sheets Zoonoses 29 July 2020 One Health 8 May 2026 Influenza (avian and other zoonotic) 21 January 2026 More Related links: Global Influenza Strategy 2019–2030 Pandemic Influenza Preparedness (PIP) Framework

Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA Argentina + 9 more Epidemiological Update Avian Influenza A(H5) in the Americas Region - 26 August 2026 Format Situation Report Source PAHO Posted 26 Aug 2026 Originally published 26 Aug 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 829.05 KB) Avian influenza A(H5) is a highly contagious viral disease that primarily affects poultry and wild birds, with the ability to sporadically infect mammalian species, including humans. Since 1996, the A/goose/Guangdong/1/96 lineage has caused recurrent outbreaks in bird populations, as well as hundreds of human cases and deaths resulting from exposure to infected animals or contaminated environments. Currently, the A(H5N1) subtype and other avian influenza A(H5) viruses have been identified in birds and mammals across multiple geographic regions worldwide. Between 2021 and March 2026, more than 600 species of wild and poultry birds and more than 100 species of mammals have been reported as affected by avian influenza viruses with zoonotic potential, such as A(H5Nx). In May 2026, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH), and the World Health Organization (WHO) determined that the global public health risk associated with highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses (HPAI) A(H5) belonging to the Gs/Gd lineage remains low. Similarly, for people with occupational or frequent exposure, the risk was estimated to be low to moderate. news.title_zh: 美洲地区流行病学更新 禽流感 A(H5) - 2026 年 8 月 26 日 - ReliefWeb
news.source_body_en: This report, published by ReliefWeb on 26 August 2026, provides an epidemiological update on avian influenza A(H5) viruses in the Americas region. It highlights that since 1996, the A/goose/Guangdong/1/96 lineage has caused recurrent outbreaks in bird populations and resulted in hundreds of human cases and deaths due to exposure to infected animals or environments. The current update notes that A(H5N1) and other avian influenza A(H5) viruses have been identified in birds and mammals across multiple geographic regions worldwide. Between 2021 and March 2026, over 600 bird species and more than 100 mammal species have been reported as affected by avian influenza viruses with zoonotic potential, such as A(H5Nx). The global public health risk associated with highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5) viruses is assessed as low, with the risk for people with occupational or frequent exposure estimated to be low to moderate. The report is an update from PAHO, indicating ongoing monitoring and assessment of the situation, with no mention of active containment measures or further investigation.

news.content: Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages Search Search All Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages July 30, 2026 - August 28, 2026 GO Home World News Mon, Aug 24, 2026 page5 Australia confirms H5N1 bird flu case in fur seal Reuters, SYDNEY Add TT as Preferred Source Australia yesterday confirmed its first case of H5N1 bird flu in a mammal, with the deadly virus found in a long-nosed fur seal in South Australia. Australia has been grappling with rising cases of the highly pathogenic avian influenza after it landed in the country in June. The country’s first mass seabird deaths from the virus occurred this month, marking an escalation of the outbreak that began after the virus was first detected in migratory seabirds before spreading to native species. South Australian authorities confirmed the nation’s first mammalian detection in the seal, found at the coastal town of Beachport, about 310 km south of Adelaide, the state capital. A fur seal suns itself on harbor steps in front of the Sydney Opera House in Australia on Oct. 2, 2014. Photo: AP The seal, one of an estimated population of 100,000 in the state’s waters, was found dead with no signs of injury, the authorities said. Its death “does not appear to be associated with other sick or dead marine mammals,” Australian Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Julie Collins said in televised remarks. “Once the H5 bird flu is spreading in the natural environment it is not possible to avoid significant losses,” she said. Australia was the last continent to report bird flu, although the virus was detected late last year on the subantarctic territory of Heard Island. More than 13,000 baby seals were killed by the virus on the island, local media reported. Seals are at high risk of contracting the virus because they live near wild birds on rocky outcrops on the coast, South Australia Department of Primary Industries and Regions Chief Veterinary Officer Skye Fruean said. “They would be coming across, no doubt, really high levels of the virus in their environment,” Fruean said in televised remarks. H5N1 has not shown up in Australia’s poultry or agriculture, according to the federal government, which on Friday said that 297 cases had been confirmed nationwide. analysis.brief_en: Australia has confirmed its first case of H5N1 bird flu in a mammal, a long-nosed fur seal found dead in Beachport, South Australia. The virus, which has been spreading in the natural environment, was first detected in migratory seabirds before moving to native species. South Australian authorities reported the case, noting that the seal’s death does not appear linked to other sick marine mammals. The Australian Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, Julie Collins, emphasized the difficulty of avoiding significant losses once the virus is established in the environment. H5N1 has not been found in Australia’s poultry or agriculture, with 297 confirmed cases nationwide. Seals are at high risk due to their coastal habitat and proximity to wild birds. The outbreak, which began in June, has led to mass seabird deaths this month, highlighting the growing threat of the virus to wildlife and ecosystems.

news.content_title: Outlook India
news.content: WHO warns of rising H5N1 bird outbreaks across Asia-Pacific. India is urged to strengthen surveillance and One Health coordination, though human H5N1 transmission remains rare. Just as India is gearing up to tackle a seasonal influenza wave, with H1N1 or swine flu cases drawing attention, the World Health Organisation (WHO) has sounded a fresh warning on another influenza threat — highly pathogenic avian influenza A (H5N1). The warning comes amid a spurt in outbreaks of H5N1 among birds in countries across the Asia-Pacific region, raising concerns over the possibility of the virus spilling over from animals to humans. The WHO has now urged countries to strengthen surveillance and ensure their health systems are ready to detect and respond rapidly to any human infections. The message came after more than 150 influenza experts, laboratory scientists and public-health officials met virtually from August 25 to 27 for the 19th Biregional Meeting of National Influenza Centres and Influenza Surveillance, jointly organised by WHO’s South-East Asia and Western Pacific regional offices. The timing is significant for India, which is already monitoring seasonal influenza. The National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) maintains dedicated surveillance and technical guidance for seasonal influenza, including H1N1, and its latest update was issued on August 11. But H5N1 is a different threat. While seasonal influenza viruses such as H1N1 circulate primarily among humans, H5N1 is an avian influenza virus that primarily affects birds and can occasionally infect humans, particularly following exposure to infected animals or contaminated environments. WHO says zoonotic influenza viruses can cause illness ranging from mild flu-like symptoms to severe respiratory disease and death. The latest WHO meeting placed particular emphasis on the spread of highly pathogenic H5N1 in birds in the Pacific and recent incursions reported in Australia and New Zealand. Swine Flu Accounts For 98% Of Tested Cases In India, No Deaths: ICMR H1N1 Cases in Delhi: Swine Flu Infections Rise In National Capital, Health Ministry Urges Early Medical Attention H1N1 Cases Rise, But No Need To Panic; Doctors Urge Vaccination For High-Risk Groups As JP Nadda Reviews Preparedness Centre Deploys National Joint Outbreak Response Team Amid Chandipura Virus Outbreak WHO stressed that the response cannot be left to the health sector alone. Animal health, human health and environmental authorities need to work together under the One Health approach to detect potential spillovers early and contain them before they become a wider public-health threat. “Australia and New Zealand’s recent experience is a sharp reminder that vigilance cannot lapse,” said Dr Saia Ma’u Piukala, WHO Regional Director for the Western Pacific, stressing the importance of coordination between human, animal and environmental health authorities. WHO, along with the Food and Agriculture Organisation, UN Environment Programme, World Organisation for Animal Health and Pacific Community, has also undertaken a Rapid Joint One Health Risk Assessment to assess the risk of H5N1 entering Pacific Island countries and identify preparedness measures. For India, the warning is relevant because influenza surveillance cannot operate in isolation from developments in animal populations. Early detection depends on being able to identify unusual infections, characterise viruses and share information rapidly between human and animal health systems. India showcased its own surveillance experience at the WHO meeting, highlighting the integration of influenza surveillance into the Integrated Health Information Platform. The system provides near-real-time data for analysing influenza trends and supporting faster outbreak detection and response. The WHO's latest global respiratory-virus update also shows that influenza activity is not uniformly high worldwide. However, elevated influenza positivity has been reported in parts of South and South-East Asia and several other regions, reinforcing the need for continued surveillance. The distinction between H1N1 and H5N1 is therefore important. A rise in seasonal H1N1 does not mean H5N1 is spreading among people. WHO continues to describe avian influenza viruses as distinct from seasonal human influenza viruses, with human transmission remaining an important point of surveillance rather than something to assume from animal outbreaks alone. The WHO meeting repeatedly returned to one message: collecting data is not enough unless it leads to timely action. “Surveillance data only matter when they change what public health systems do,” said Dr Gina Samaan, WHO Regional Emergency Director for the Western Pacific. The region is consequently being urged to strengthen laboratory capacity, genomic sequencing, timely sharing of influenza viruses and data, and the ability to rapidly characterise unusual strains. The broader concern is preparedness. H5N1 has been causing unprecedented levels of disease and deaths among wild birds and poultry in several parts of the world since the emergence of the H5 clade 2.3.4.4b viruses in 2020. Human infections remain rare, but when they occur, they can be severe. For India, the immediate public-health priority remains keeping a close watch on seasonal influenza and ensuring appropriate diagnosis and treatment. But the WHO alert is also a reminder that influenza preparedness cannot stop at human hospitals. “Our strength is in our network – in sharing expertise, information and capacities, and in supporting one another to be better prepared for the threats ahead,” said Dr Nilesh Buddha, Officer-in-Charge for the WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia. “Where expertise exists in one country, we should facilitate its transfer and application across the region; where specialised capacities are available, we should strengthen pathways for countries to access them.” Dr Buddha also stressed the importance of coordinated investments, resource mobilisation and strategic prioritisation at a time when resources are increasingly constrained. He called for greater collaboration to make optimal use of existing capacities, maximise impact and avoid duplication. From 2003 to August 2025, the WHO has reported 990 human H5N1 cases across 25 countries, including 475 deaths – a 48% fatality rate. In humans, H5N1 infection can resemble a severe bout of influenza, with symptoms such as high fever, cough, sore throat and muscle aches, while some infected people may remain symptom-free. Although the risk to the general population remains low, health authorities are closely monitoring the virus for any changes that could increase its ability to spread among humans, according to reports

news.source_body_en: The World Health Organisation (WHO) has issued an alert about the rising threat of H5N1 bird flu in the Asia-Pacific region, emphasizing the need for vigilance and preparedness. This warning comes amid a surge in outbreaks among birds, particularly in Australia and New Zealand, and highlights the importance of the One Health approach to monitor and respond to potential spillovers from animals to humans. While H5N1 can cause severe illness and death in humans, transmission remains rare. The WHO has urged countries to strengthen surveillance, laboratory capacity, and data sharing to detect and respond to any human infections promptly. India, which is already monitoring seasonal influenza, is being called upon to integrate its surveillance efforts with those in animal and environmental health sectors. From 2003 to August 2025, the WHO reported 990 human H5N1 cases across 25 countries, with 475 deaths, indicating a high fatality rate. However, the risk to the general population remains low. The WHO meeting stressed the importance of timely action based on surveillance data and called for greater collaboration to optimize existing capacities and avoid duplication.

We know how bad this can get Published: August 23, 2026 4:16am EDT Australia has crossed another grim threshold in its H5N1 bird flu outbreak. For the first time, the virus has infected an Australian mainland mammal: a long-nosed fur seal found dead at Beachport on South Australia’s Limestone Coast, about a four-hour drive southeast of Adelaide. This is a devastating development, although sadly not an unexpected one. H5N1 is already circulating in wild seabirds along the Limestone Coast, with many infected greater crested terns found at Beachport itself. This seal likely caught the virus through contact with either infected birds or the environment they share. As of today, there is no evidence that it is part of a wider marine mammal outbreak. One infected seal is not a seal outbreak. But we know from overseas just how quickly that can change. We know how bad this can get When H5N1 reached southern elephant seals in Argentina in 2023 more than 17,000 pups died. At one intensively monitored colony, mortality eventually reached 95%. Genetic evidence strongly supported transmission between mammals, rather than thousands of seals independently becoming infected from birds. The devastation followed the virus into the Southern Ocean. On South Georgia island (east of the Falkland Islands), the number of breeding female southern elephant seals fell by 47% between 2022 and 2024, following the arrival of H5N1. Dead elephant seals in South Georgia, seen in early 2025 during the bird flu outbreak on the island. Jane Younger Then, at Australia’s Heard Island (about 1,700 km north of Antarctica), an estimated 13,359 elephant seal pups are believed to have died during the 2025 outbreak. Antarctic fur seals have also been hit extremely hard. Field observations suggest they may have suffered the greatest number of deaths of any species, although the scale of the outbreaks makes a reliable total impossible. These are not isolated animal deaths. For already threatened species – such as the Australian sea lion, the Antarctic fur seal and the southern elephant seal – losses on this scale can push species closer to extinction. What is a long-nosed fur seal – and what happens next? Long-nosed fur seals, formerly known as New Zealand fur seals, occur in Western Australia, South Australia, Tasmania and New Zealand. The South Australian population is estimated at around 100,000 individuals. We do not know exactly how the Beachport seal became infected, but infection could occur through direct contact with infected birds or other seals, or exposure to contaminated beaches or water. Australia is also home to Australian fur seals and the endangered Australian sea lion, a species found nowhere else on Earth. Its entire population is estimated at fewer than 12,000 animals, around 85% of them in South Australia. H5N1-infected birds have already been found at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island, while mass bird deaths are occurring at the South Australian island group The Pages – both important Australian sea lion breeding locations. Australia’s Macquarie Island (about 1,500 km southeast of Tasmania) is also home to southern elephant seals and endangered Antarctic fur seals – both species that have faced huge losses from H5N1 in other parts of the world. Seal populations now need urgent surveillance. We can’t stop H5N1 spreading through a colony, but we need to know where it is, how quickly it is spreading and which populations are being hardest hit. Why are seals so vulnerable? Seals gather on the coast in dense colonies, in close contact with each other and in contaminated ground and water, creating opportunities for rapid transmission. But the biology of the virus matters too. H5N1 is fundamentally a bird virus, but the lineage that spread through marine mammals in South America acquired mutations that improve its ability to replicate in the cells of mammals. Our recent research (yet to have been peer reviewed) found that H5N1 continued to evolve as it spread through seals, including more changes that help it replicate in mammals. But severe outbreaks in seals also occurred without these changes, suggesting seals may be particularly vulnerable to the virus. We do not yet know which viral lineage infected the Beachport seal. Rapid genome sequencing will be important to determine whether it carries the mammalian-adaptive mutations seen overseas. Australia needs a seal plan now There are currently no commercially available H5 vaccines suitable for mammals available in Australia. But there is promising overseas work. In the United States, researchers tested a vaccine – originally developed for dairy cattle – in northern elephant seals. The vaccine was well tolerated and produced a clear, measurable antibody response. Researchers then extended the trial to endangered Hawaiian monk seals in rehabilitation. This does not yet amount to a vaccination program for free-ranging seals, and the vaccine does not have regulatory approval for use in Australia. Vaccinating every seal colony would also be impossible. Fur seals typically enter the water as soon as people approach, making vaccination infeasible for this species. But Australia should urgently investigate whether targeted vaccination could protect select populations where intervention is both feasible and worthwhile – particularly endangered Australian sea lions, and southern elephant seals on Macquarie Island, which remains an enormously important Australian breeding population. Vaccination will never stop H5N1 spreading through wildlife. But it may help prevent catastrophic losses in the species we can reach. The Beachport seal is one animal – for now. But this virus has already shown us what can happen next. Australia should use that warning while we still have time. Please do not touch sick or dead birds or marine mammals. Record the location, take photographs from a safe distance, keep pets away, and report the sighting to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888. The situation underscores the risks of H5N1 to marine mammals and the importance of monitoring its spread to prevent catastrophic losses in endangered populations.

news.source_body_en: The article reports the first confirmed death of an H5N1 bird flu-infected long-nosed fur seal on Australian mainland, found dead at Beachport on South Australia’s Limestone Coast. This marks a critical development in the ongoing H5N1 outbreak, as the virus has previously caused severe mortality in seals in Argentina and South Georgia. The seal likely contracted the virus through contact with infected birds or contaminated environments. While there is no evidence of a wider marine mammal outbreak in Australia, the potential for rapid spread is highlighted, especially given the dense seal colonies and shared habitats with infected birds. The article stresses the need for urgent surveillance and research into targeted vaccination strategies for vulnerable species like the Australian sea lion and southern elephant seals on Macquarie Island. However, no approved vaccines are currently available for use in Australia, and the exact viral lineage responsible for the Beachport infection remains undetermined. The situation underscores the risks of H5N1 to marine mammals and the importance of monitoring its spread to prevent catastrophic losses in endangered populations.

Photograph: David C Tomlinson/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A fur seal, similar to this one seen sleeping in New Zealand, is the first confirmed mammal death from the deadly H5 bird flu strain on the Australian mainland. Photograph: David C Tomlinson/Getty Images Fur seal’s death marks first Australian mainland mammal fatality from spreading H5 bird flu strain Seal found dead at Beachport in South Australia presages ‘significant losses’, minister warns Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast A long-nosed fur seal has died from H5 bird flu in South Australia, marking the first confirmed case in a mammal on the Australian mainland. The seal was found dead at Beachport on Wednesday on the state’s Limestone Coast. It marks a fresh escalation in the spread of the virus days after the South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, announced three mass mortality events on offshore islands involving more than 1,000 greater crested terns. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The federal agriculture minister, Julie Collins, said the seal death was “not unexpected” as the virus begins to spread through the country. Speaking in Hobart on Sunday, Collins said the “distressing” news of the first confirmed case of a mammal on the mainland was anticipated and that it was “not possible to avoid significant losses”. “An infection of this individual animal is likely to have occurred due to exposure to infected wild birds or the environment that they share,” she said. “We can’t stop it spreading in terms of, particularly, in wild birds, and where we see more dead wild birds, we do expect to see increased reports of marine mammals.” Collins said there had been 298 events across the country, with 183 in South Australia, 86 in Victoria, 11 in New South Wales, 10 in Western Australia, seven in Tasmania and one in Queensland. The risk of human transmission remains low, but people are being urged to avoid sick or dead birds and report them to birdflu.gov.au. ‘Devastating’: Western Australia fears a black swan moment as bird flu threatens flagship species Read more The long-nosed fur seal was found dead with no signs of injury and reported to an official hotline by a member of the public on Wednesday Testing of samples from the seal later confirmed the H5 bird flu detection. The highly pathogenic strain of bird flu has killed millions of birds globally and crossed over into mammal species, including elephant seals. Long-nosed fur seals and the endangered Australian sea lion are among the mammal species the federal government has assessed as facing very high risk from the virus. Jack Gough, the chief executive of the Invasive Species Council, said the virus spreading to Australia’s sea lion population could be an “extinction level event”. “We are still just at the early stages of this devastating virus, and the bad news is going to keep coming for our wildlife as it spreads around the continent and between species,” he said. The SA government has also confirmed a little penguin found at Kangaroo Island this week tested positive for H5 bird flu. The SA’s environment minister, Emily Bourke, said the state would work with the federal government to assess whether an experimental vaccine from the United States could be used for mammals in Australia. “It is not an off-the-shelf vaccine that’s been approved, and we have to be taking into consideration the risk [of undertaking] the vaccination program in our mammals,” she said. Australian Marine Conservation Society campaign director, Alexia Wellbelove, urged the federal government to create a $200m wildlife resilience fund for threatened species at risk of mass mortalities or local extinctions. “Government preparedness funding got us this far, but it was never designed to manage active spread across multiple species and states,” Wellbelove said. Elsewhere, the Tasmanian government said 51 little penguins found on the state’s King Island were “assumed to” have died from H5 bird flu, but the deaths would not be declared a mass mortality event. The state’s natural resources and environment department said a sample taken from one penguin found at the Port of Grassy tested positive for H5 bird flu, while a sample from a second penguin was inconclusive. Wes Ford, the state’s incident controller for its bird flu response, said both samples had been sent to the Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness for further testing. “The little penguin mortality event is not considered a mass mortality event, and the condition of the remaining deceased birds meant they were unsuitable for testing,” he said. “As a result, the cause of death could not be confirmed, although it may be assumed to have been from bird flu. “Our teams continue to monitor reports of sick and dead birds closely, with results from surveillance informing our response.” Explore more on these topics Bird flu South Australia news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Senator calls for criminal investigation of RFK Jr after Guardian report Dolly Parton obituary Warning of fresh danger from rising lake water in Nepal – as it happened Ukraine war briefing: Missiles shot down during long Russian attack wave Jon Ossoff went low on Natalie Harp. analysis.brief_en: A long-nosed fur seal found dead at Beachport in South Australia has tested positive for H5 bird flu, marking the first confirmed mammal fatality from the virus on the Australian mainland. The event was reported by The Guardian on August 23, 2026, and confirmed by the South Australian government. The H5 bird flu has been spreading across the country, with 298 events recorded, including 183 in South Australia, 86 in Victoria, and others in New South Wales, Western Australia, Tasmania, and Queensland. The virus has already caused mass mortality events in offshore islands, with over 1,000 greater crested terns affected. The federal agriculture minister, Julie Collins, stated that the spread of the virus to mammals is not unexpected and warned of significant losses. The risk of human transmission remains low, but authorities are urging people to avoid contact with sick or dead birds and report them. The South Australian environment minister, Emily Bourke, is considering the use of an experimental vaccine from the United States for mammals, though it is not yet approved. The virus has also been detected in little penguins on Kangaroo Island, with some deaths assumed to be from H5 bird flu. The spread of the virus to marine mammals like long-nosed fur seals and Australian sea lions raises concerns about potential extinction events, as these species are at very high risk. The government is monitoring the situation closely and is working to implement a response strategy.

news.title_zh: 海狗的死亡标志着澳大利亚大陆首例因 H​​5 禽流感病毒传播而死亡的哺乳动物 - 卫报
news.source_body_en: A long-nosed fur seal found dead at Beachport in South Australia has tested positive for H5 bird flu, marking the first confirmed mammal fatality from the virus on the Australian mainland. The event was reported by The Guardian on August 23, 2026, and confirmed by the South Australian government. The H5 bird flu has been spreading across the country, with 298 events recorded, including 183 in South Australia, 86 in Victoria, and others in New South Wales, Western Australia, Tasmania, and Queensland. The virus has already caused mass mortality events in offshore islands, with over 1,000 greater crested terns affected. The federal agriculture minister, Julie Collins, stated that the spread of the virus to mammals is not unexpected and warned of significant losses. The risk of human transmission remains low, but authorities are urging people to avoid contact with sick or dead birds and report them. The South Australian environment minister, Emily Bourke, is considering the use of an experimental vaccine from the United States for mammals, though it is not yet approved. The virus has also been detected in little penguins on Kangaroo Island, with some deaths assumed to be from H5 bird flu. The spread of the virus to marine mammals like long-nosed fur seals and Australian sea lions raises concerns about potential extinction events, as these species are at very high risk. The government is monitoring the situation closely and is working to implement a response strategy.
news.content_zh: 南澳大利亚海滩港发现的一只长鼻毛皮海豹的 H5 禽流感检测呈阳性,这是澳大利亚大陆首例确诊的哺乳动物死于该病毒的病例。《卫报》于 2026 年 8 月 23 日报道了这一事件,并得到了南澳大利亚州政府的证实。H5禽流感已在全国范围内蔓延,已记录298起事件,其中南澳大利亚州183起,维多利亚州86起,新南威尔士州、西澳大利亚州、塔斯马尼亚州和昆士兰州有其他事件。该病毒已在近海岛屿引发大规模 死亡率 事件,超过 1,000 只大凤头燕鸥受到影响。联邦农业部长朱莉·柯林斯表示,病毒向哺乳动物传播并不意外,并警告称可能会造成重大损失。人类感染 传播 的风险仍然很低,但当局敦促人们避免接触病鸟或死鸟并进行报告。南澳大利亚环境部长 Emily Bourke 正在考虑将来自美国的实验性 疫苗 用于哺乳动物,但尚未获得批准。袋鼠岛的小企鹅身上也发现了这种病毒,一些企鹅的死亡被认为是死于 H5 禽流感。该病毒向长鼻海狗和澳大利亚海狮等海洋哺乳动物的传播引起了人们对潜在灭绝事件的担忧,因为这些物种面临着非常高的风险。政府正在密切关注事态发展,并正在努力实施应对策略。

news.content: Menu About Us Newsletter Investor Q&A Agtech FoodTech Deeptech Video Can smarter surveillance help poultry farms catch bird flu earlier? August 25, 2026 | Elaine Watson Agtech Deeptech Livestock/animal ag Wildfowl can shed avian flu viruses in their saliva, nasal secretions, and feces, infecting nearby poultry farms. Image credit: istock/arlutz73 Rapid on-farm pathogen testing firm Alveo Technologies has teamed up with wildfowl surveillance specialist AgriNerds to create an early warning system for avian flu it claims could dramatically improve poultry farmers’ ability to detect and contain outbreaks before they escalate. The partnership combines AgriNerds’ Waterfowl Alert Network—which uses radar, satellite imagery, telemetry (radio tags to track wild birds), and other data to predict where infection risk is highest from wild birds—with Alveo’s portable molecular diagnostics platform, which can detect avian flu in 45 minutes. The aim is to find a middle ground between impractical, round-the-clock “super-surveillance” and waiting for birds to show symptoms before testing and then waiting another two to three days for PCR lab results—by which point the virus may already have spread within and beyond the farm. Instead, producers could step up testing when AgriNerds’ model signals that migratory bird activity or other factors have increased the likelihood of infection, Alveo president Erik Tyrrell-Knott told AgFunderNews. Data generated by Alveo’s tests—which are already on the market in several countries and on track to secure USDA approval later this year—can in turn feed back into AgriNerds’ models and potentially make subsequent risk predictions more precise. “Right now, if egg production goes down, if the birds appear lethargic, or the mortality rate goes up, farmers have a decision to make,” said Tyrrell-Knott. “It might be bird flu. It might be something else. Are you going to incur a lot of expense and take all these [extra] biosecurity measures flying blind, or are you going to wait days [for lab test results] and it’s business as usual [in the meantime]? “We’ve got two 21st century technologies combining to provide informed, intelligent, data-driven surveillance guidance, which is something that is totally missing in the current landscape.” AgriNerds has developed a predictive tool for determining waterfowl abundance in close proximity to commercial poultry. Image credit: AgriNerds Grading risk for dynamic surveillance Waterfowl are a major reservoir of bird flu, creating a risk when infected birds fly over or roost near poultry farms. AgriNerds combines multiple data sources to predict waterfowl abundance close to individual poultry facilities and classifies risk as low, moderate, or high. While seasonal migration patterns are broadly predictable, the risk surrounding individual farms can vary significantly from one year to the next as weather, crops, water availability and habitat change, said AgriNerds founder Maurice Pitesky, an associate professor at the UC Davis Weill school of veterinary medicine. Generally, he said, wild birds are looking for a food source and a water source. And both can be subject to change, for example should a nearby farmer plant new or different crops, or should heavy rain create an environment that might attract waterfowl. The network now makes daily predictions across the country relative to 160,000+ commercial poultry facilities, said Pitesky, who says AgriNerds’ data is now used by 1,500+ farms across 25 states. “The farm doesn’t change location, but the risk does change.” Users could, for example, choose only to receive alerts when a farm enters the highest-risk category. “The vet wakes up and is notified in real time: You’ve got a red day today.” What does earlier detection actually change? But what is the value of early detection if infected flocks must ultimately be destroyed? For infected birds, says Tyrrell-Knott, there’s not much you can do. But if you catch bird flu early, you can restrict movements of employees, feed and waste trucks, and take other measures aimed at limiting farm-to-farm transmission. Farms can also modify ventilation practices designed to limit the dispersal of potentially contaminated material. This is particularly important because infection does not only move from wild birds into poultry operations but in about 30% of cases is spread from farm to farm through people, vehicles, equipment or airborne material, he claimed. Pitesky said Alveo’s results could also add much more granular disease data to AgriNerds’ risk model. Rather than relying on bird flu detections reported at county level, it could potentially incorporate geotagged test results from individual farms and combine these with wind direction and other environmental information. “If you have an on-farm test that comes back positive, we can understand where feather dander might be traveling from infected facilities and warn farms that are downwind.” Longer term, more rapid testing combined with more detailed intelligence on bird movements could reduce the overall number of birds that have to be culled in a large facility if early detection means the virus can be contained within one barn, said Tyrrell-Knott. “We believe in future with our accuracy, our sensitivity, the rapidity and trustworthiness of our results, that you could start to partially depopulate some of these complexes when you’ve got 13 barns with two million birds on a complex, instead of having to cull all the birds.” Alveo is deploying “basically the same molecular amplification technology [used in a laboratory],” says the firm. “But we’ve reduced it to the size of a cell phone and made it rugged, easy to use and affordable.” Image credit: Alveo Technologies Testing asymptomatic flocks Alveo’s platform uses molecular amplification rather than the lateral-flow technology used in rapid strip tests, which are not hugely reliable, claimed Tyrrell-Knott. “It’s rapid, but 30-40% of the time they miss the virus, so you get a false negative.” Alveo, by contrast, is deploying “basically the same molecular amplification technology [used in a laboratory],” said Tyrrell-Knott. “But we’ve reduced it to the size of a cell phone and made it rugged, easy to use and affordable.” The tech can distinguish between H5 and H7 subtypes of avian influenza at 96-99% accuracy, approaching what you’d get from PCR tests in a lab, results from which can take 2-3 days to arrive, he claimed. In the US, the Alveo test currently being evaluated uses oropharyngeal swabs, while outside the US Alveo also uses cloacal swabs from the birds’ rear end, says the firm. Building an early-warning network The broader opportunity is to shift bird flu management further upstream, from responding to outbreaks after they occur toward identifying when farms are exposed to unusually high external risk and testing accordingly, said Pitesky. “In this way, agriculture can move past reactive disease management to adopt a proactive, risk-informed approach.” Tyrrell-Knott added: “We’ve been approved for experimental use by the USDA and state vets and we believe we’re on track for approval in Q4 of this year as the first on farm molecular bird flu test in the US. We’re not allowed to pre-sell but we spoke at a big poultry conference in Texas a few weeks ago and we were mobbed.” Share this article LinkedInXFacebookEmail Sign up for our weekly newsletter. news.title_zh: 更智能的监测能否帮助家禽养殖场更早感染禽流感? - AgFunderNews
news.source_body_en: On August 25, 2026, AgFunderNews reported that Alveo Technologies and AgriNerds have partnered to develop an early warning system for avian flu. This system combines AgriNerds’ Waterfowl Alert Network, which uses radar, satellite imagery, and telemetry to predict infection risk from wild birds, with Alveo’s portable molecular diagnostics platform capable of detecting avian flu in 45 minutes. The aim is to enable poultry farmers to take proactive measures, such as restricting movements and modifying ventilation, to limit farm-to-farm transmission. Alveo’s test, which uses molecular amplification technology, is currently under USDA evaluation and is expected to be approved by Q4 2026. The system is designed to provide real-time alerts and improve disease management by integrating on-farm test results with environmental data, potentially reducing the need for large-scale culling. However, the value of early detection remains debated, as infected birds may still require culling, and the system is not yet in widespread use.
news.content_zh: 2026 年 8 月 25 日,AgFunderNews 报道 Alveo Technologies 和 AgriNerds 合作开发禽流感预警系统。该系统结合了 AgriNerds 的水禽警报网络(该网络使用雷达、卫星图像和遥测技术来预测 野生鸟类 的感染风险)与 Alveo 的便携式分子诊断平台(能够在 45 分钟内检测禽流感)。其目的是使家禽养殖户能够采取主动措施,例如限制活动和改变通风,以限制农场之间的 传播。Alveo 的测试采用分子扩增技术,目前正在接受美国农业部的评估,预计将于 2026 年第四季度获得批准。该系统旨在通过将农场测试结果与环境数据相结合来提供实时警报并改善疾病管理,从而可能减少大规模扑杀的需要。然而,早期检测的价值仍然存在争议,因为受感染的鸟类可能仍然需要扑杀,而且该系统尚未广泛使用。

news.content: You need to enable JavaScript to run this app. Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Iran warUkraineGerman car industry Latest audioLatest videos Live TV Advertisement HealthAustralia Australia confirms H5N1 bird flu case in local mammal Mahima Kapoor with Reuters 08/23/2026August 23, 2026 Australian authorities said the deadly virus's spread to mammals was "concerning" but "not unexpected." https://p.dw.com/p/5JGde Copy link Australia has been grappling with bird flu since JuneImage: Phillip Island Nature Parks/AFP Advertisement Australia confirmed its first case of H5N1 bird flu in a mammal on Sunday, after it found the deadly virus in a long-nosed fur seal. Authorities in the state of South Australia said they found the virus in the seal in the coastal town of Beachport, about 310 kilometers (192 miles) from the state capital, Adelaide. Austrialia has been combating the highly pathogenic influenza after it arrived in the country in June. Earlier this month it reported its first mass seabird deaths, marking an escalation. What did authorities have to say? There are an estimated 100,000 long-nosed fur seals in the state's waters. The infected individual was found dead with no signs of injury, authorities said. Its death "does not appear to be associated with other sick or dead marine mammals," Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said in televised remarks. "Once the H5 bird flu is spreading in the natural environment it is not possible to avoid significant losses," Collins added. "Although this is a concerning development, it is not unexpected for us to start to see infection in other wildlife, particularly in marine mammals, particularly in areas where there are high infection rates in wild birds," Collins was quoted by the Australian Broadcasting Corporation as saying. Australia began vaccinating its birds against the deadly virus earlier this monthImage: Phillip Island Nature Parks/AFP The virus has not spread to Australia's poultry or agriculture, according to the government, which counted 297 confirmed cases as of Friday. Earlier in August, the government said it would begin a bird vaccination program based on the species' vulnerability to the virus and conservation impact. analysis.location_and_population: The case was confirmed in Beachport, a coastal town in South Australia, approximately 310 kilometers from Adelaide. The affected population includes long-nosed fur seals, with an estimated 100,000 in the state's waters.

analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Australia's authorities are actively investigating the spread of H5N1 bird flu, including its impact on wildlife. analysis.brief_en: Australia confirmed its first case of H5N1 bird flu in a mammal, specifically a long-nosed fur seal, on August 23, 2026. The seal was found dead in Beachport, South Australia, approximately 310 kilometers from Adelaide. The authorities described the spread of the virus to mammals as concerning but not unexpected, noting that H5N1 has been spreading in the natural environment. The government has initiated a bird vaccination program and reported 297 confirmed cases as of Friday, with no spread to poultry or agriculture. Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins emphasized that the virus's presence in marine mammals is a natural progression, especially in areas with high infection rates in wild birds. The case highlights the ongoing threat of H5N1 bird flu and the need for continued monitoring and preventive measures.

Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu USDA confirms new H5N1 avian flu cases in poultry, dairy cattle News brief Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Avian Influenza (Bird Flu) Share Copied to clipboard Clara Bastain/iStock After nearly 30 days with no updates, the US Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) this week posted several recent H5N1 avian flu detections in both commercial poultry and dairy cattle. In the past 30 days there have been three confirmed detections in dairy cows, with Texas reporting two affected herds and Utah reporting a single detection. So far this year 85 cattle herds have had confirmed H5N1 infections. Last year APHIS tracked 171 H5N1 outbreaks in cattle. In 2024, the year the virus was first detected in cows, the United States saw 917 herds infected. Poultry operation hit South Dakota is reporting a large H5N1 outbreak among commercial poultry breeding operations in Edmunds County, according to a separate APHIS tracker, with 29,700 birds affected. South Dakota reported another outbreak in Brule County with 2,800 birds. In Idaho, two smaller outbreaks were confirmed in birds in Ada and Canyon counties. In the past 30 days, APHIS has confirmed outbreaks in two commercial and three backyard US flocks. CDC, FDA end investigation into Listeria outbreak, begin looking into new Salmonella cluster News brief Mary Van Beusekom, MS Topics Foodborne Disease Listeria Salmonella Cyclospora Marta Miranda / Flickr cc As the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) end their investigation into the June Listeria outbreak tied to soft cheese, the FDA is reporting a new outbreak, this one involving Salmonella from an unidentified food source. The CDC has also released updated case counts for several smaller Cyclospora outbreaks. New 84-case Salmonella Newport outbreak Yesterday, the two agencies declared the four-state Listeria monocytogenes outbreak traced to soft cheese over after reporting three new cases and four new hospitalizations, for a total of 15 and 14, respectively. One person died. The cheese manufacturer, Maryland-based Clover Hill Dairy, recalled its ricotta-like requeson cheese and all other cheese products in June. Also yesterday, the FDA reported a new 84-case Salmonella Newport outbreak tied to a yet-to-be-identified food source. No other details have been released. The FDA updated case counts for three Cyclospora outbreaks with unknown food sources, adding five, two, and one cases, for totals of 22, 203, and 28, respectively. The case total for all US summer Cyclospora outbreaks, including the one linked to contaminated iceberg lettuce, is now 17,180 after the CDC added 3,285 infections this week. The CDC also said it is investigating another 11,844 cases that are not yet confirmed. At least two people have died of cyclosporiasis this summer, and 922 have been hospitalized. Improved hand hygiene had no impact on detection of multidrug-resistant organisms, hospital study finds News brief Chris Dall, MA Topics Healthcare-Associated Infections Yoo Chung / Flickr cc A study conducted at four hospitals in Atlanta found that improved hand hygiene had no impact on detection of multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs), researchers reported today in Infection Control & Hospital Epidemiology. For the study, a team led by researchers at Emory University School of Medicine analyzed correlations between monthly unit-level hand hygiene adherence and rates of hospital-onset MDROs and other pathogens of epidemiologic significance (MDRO+) that can cause healthcare-associated infections (HAIs). Hand hygiene adherence was determined by an electronic monitoring system in patients’ rooms that records whether a healthcare worker dispensed hand hygiene product after entering the room. The study authors note that while it’s widely accepted that high hand hygiene adherence reduces HAI incidence, many of the studies looking at the relationship between the two often rely on direct observation of hand hygiene adherence, which can be prone to overestimates. “The limitations of direct observation have generated interest in alternative methods for hand hygiene monitoring,” they wrote. “Automated hand hygiene monitoring systems (AHHMS) are an appealing solution to overcome the pitfalls of direct observation.” Complex interplay between hand hygiene, MDRO acquisition More than 22.7 million hand hygiene opportunities were recorded by the AHHMS during the study period: January 2021 through September 2022. The mean monthly hand hygiene adherence rate increased from 41% in January 2021 to 57% in September 2022 on average across all units and facilities. A total of 1,847 MDRO+ detections were observed in 752,341 patient days, with a median composite MDRO+ rate of 1.7 per 1,000 patient-days. Despite the hand hygiene improvement, the researchers were unable to demonstrate a clear unit-level inverse association between hand hygiene adherence and MDRO+ detection (rate ratio, 1.01). They say the results like reflect the “complex interaction between the two variable and unmeasured confounders.” “The interplay between hand hygiene, infection prevention efforts, and MDRO acquisition is complex, and an absence of proof does not negate the importance of hand hygiene,” they wrote. analysis.time: The US Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) confirmed new H5N1 avian flu cases in the past 30 days, with updates reported on 2026-08-27.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreaks were confirmed in commercial poultry and dairy cattle in South Dakota, Texas, and Utah, with specific mention of South Dakota's Edmunds County and Brule County, and Texas and Utah's dairy herds.
analysis.event: USDA confirmed new H5N1 avian flu cases in poultry and dairy cattle, with three confirmed detections in dairy cows and a large outbreak in South Dakota's poultry breeding operations.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: So far this year, 85 cattle herds have had confirmed H5N1 infections. In South Dakota, 29,700 birds were affected in one outbreak, and 2,800 in another. Last year, APHIS tracked 171 H5N1 outbreaks in cattle, and in 2024, 917 herds were infected.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The USDA is actively tracking and confirming H5N1 outbreaks in cattle and poultry. No further details on specific measures or risk assessments were provided.

analysis.brief_en: The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) confirmed new H5N1 avian flu cases in both commercial poultry and dairy cattle, with recent updates reported on August 27, 2026. In South Dakota, a large outbreak affected 29,700 birds in Edmunds County, and another 2,800 birds were impacted in Brule County. Additionally, three dairy cow herds in Texas and Utah were confirmed to have H5N1 infections. This year, 85 cattle herds have been infected with H5N1, compared to 171 in the same period last year and 917 in 2024. The USDA is actively monitoring these outbreaks, but no further details on specific response measures or risk assessments were provided. The outbreaks highlight the ongoing spread of H5N1 among livestock, raising concerns about potential impacts on animal health and food safety.

This year, 85 cattle herds have been infected with H5N1, compared to 171 in the same period last year and 917 in 2024. The USDA is actively monitoring these outbreaks, but no further details on specific response measures or risk assessments were provided. The outbreaks highlight the ongoing spread of H5N1 among livestock, raising concerns about potential impacts on animal health and food safety.

Experts suggest that stopping feeding is the safest approach, though smaller amounts of food may be acceptable. The findings are based on observations and expert recommendations rather than confirmed data. The study emphasizes the need for caution in managing bird feeders to mitigate the risk of disease transmission among avian populations.

File photo: Reuters. Sydney, Aug. 23 (SANA) Australia on Sunday confirmed its first H5N1 bird flu case in a mammal after the virus was detected in a long-nosed fur seal found dead in Beachport, South Australia. Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said the seal was found without visible injuries and its death did not appear linked to illness or deaths among other marine mammals, according to the Australian News Agency. Collins warned that the virus spreading in the natural environment could cause significant wildlife losses. The case comes amid increasing H5N1 infections among wild birds, with mass seabird deaths recorded in South Australia. Authorities have confirmed hundreds of cases among birds, while no infections have been detected in poultry or livestock. The risk to human health remains low, according to Australian health and veterinary authorities. The virus reached Australia this year through migratory birds, prompting increased wildlife monitoring for its possible spread to other species. Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/AAP View image in fullscreen The black swan, which has come to define the west, has been ranked as ‘very high risk’ of becoming infected with the bird flu virus. Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/AAP ‘Devastating’: Western Australia fears a black swan moment as bird flu threatens flagship species The state’s bird emblem is an indicator species for H5N1, with high visibility populations and low survival rates. Experts are warning of ‘significant mortality’ Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast When the black swans start dying, Western Australians will know that bird flu has truly arrived. The birds are an “indicator species” because once they are infected with the H5N1 virus, they are more likely to die than survive, according to the University of Queensland virologist Kirsty Short. “If avian influenza gets into a place where there are black swans ... then I think we will see swan mortality and if there’s a significant number of swans, significant mortality.” More than 1,000 birds found dead in three mass mortality events amid ‘significant’ H5 escalation in Australia Read more WA’s black swans are deeply woven into its identity. As the state’s official bird emblem, the species is emblazoned on buildings, stamps, the flag and the coat of arms. Now the bird that has come to define the west is facing devastating consequences. Unlike many birds, black swans lack a key immune protein involved in recognising viral infections, a difference that may leave them vulnerable to a killer inflammatory response. The species has been ranked as “very high risk” of becoming infected with the virus, according to a commonwealth national risk assessment. Experts don’t yet know how black swans will respond to living with a virus that, once established, is expected to circulate and evolve in wild bird populations. ‘Potential’ to lose entire populations Black swans live in both coastal and inland freshwater areas and can form large colonies when breeding. An infected bird could cause an entire colony to die out, the ornithologist Floyd Holmes from Phoenix Environmental Sciences says. “It is not likely to wipe out all of the swans, but for any local groups of swans, particularly in the south-west, that all congregate and breed in a single place, the potential to just lose that entire population all at once is definitely there,” Holmes says. “It would be pretty devastating for that local area.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email South Australia, where the virus was first reported, has already reported three mass mortality events involving more than 1,000 greater crested terns. Holmes says the public is also more likely to notice the impacts on black swans because the birds are so large and distinctive. Nine weeks after a migratory bird brought H5N1 to WA shores – and five years after this variant of the virus reached North America – the WA government says it is now testing the vaccine in five endangered black cockatoos at Perth zoo. “The feasibility of vaccination in black swans is being explored,” the WA environment minister, Matthew Swinbourn, says. “This is just one tool in the fight against the disease.” View image in fullscreen For the Noongar people, the black swan is called Maarli or Kuljak and carries a totemic significance that predates its adoption as a state symbol. Photograph: Benny Marty/Alamy The federal agriculture minister, Julie Collins, says the government has spent $113m on bird flu preparedness, including purchasing $2m worth of vaccine to protect captive populations of priority species. The vaccine is produced by US animal health company Zoetis and was originally designed for use in chickens. It is not registered for use in wildlife and would need to be assessed before its use can be extended to native birds, Swinbourn says. The government was tight-lipped about the strength of evidence that the vaccine will work in native species. “The vaccination rollout led by states and territories has commenced and will continue across the country in the coming weeks and months,” a Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry spokesperson says. skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion Birds require two doses of the vaccine, weeks apart, so it is not feasible to vaccinate most wild populations, experts say. Efforts have begun to vaccinate 5,000 little penguins in wild colonies in Victoria, a process only considered possible because the colonies are well-studied, used to humans and return to the same burrows every night. Short says until now, there has been a lack of investment in research to understand what avian influenza and avian vaccines do in native species. “There were some studies that were done vaccinating different birds in a zoo with a H5N1 vaccine, and they found that parrots didn’t mount a very good antibody response for some reason,” Short says. “So there are obviously species-dependent variations, and I think we really should have invested in understanding what this virus means specifically for Australia.” Birds already under threat The BirdLife Australia waterbird ecologist Lindall Kidd says WA is now playing catch up after much of its bird flu preparedness funding was directed towards agriculture. “Our birds are already under pressure from habitat loss through land clearing and climate change, we could be looking at death by a thousand cuts,” she says. Bird flu has devastated wildlife around the world. What Australian birds are most at risk? Read more “There was a known gap in preparedness prior to the bird flu incursion, and we did not have enough plans in place especially for some of our more common, widely spread species. They are the ones in our urban areas, like pelicans and swans,” Kidd says. She says the psychosocial effect of losing large numbers of swans will be “massive”. For the Noongar people of south-west WA, the black swan is called Maarli or Kuljak and it carries a totemic significance that predates its adoption as a state symbol, according to Murdoch University Noongar researcher Glen Stasiuk. “With connections to brotherhood and the seasons, it is a very important bird,” Stasiuk says. While the future of WA’s bird emblem remains unknown, Holmes puts the possibilities simply. “Option one is they develop an immunity to the virus, option two is that the virus doesn’t end up reaching all of them, or option three is we lose them all,” Holmes says. “I suspect that the number of swans is going to go down. Hopefully it doesn’t reach zero. I don’t think it will, but I guess time will tell.” Explore more on these topics Western Australia Bird flu Birds Wildlife Animals features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Senator calls for criminal investigation of RFK Jr after Guardian report Dolly Parton obituary Warning of fresh danger from rising lake water in Nepal – as it happened Ukraine war briefing: Missiles shot down during long Russian attack wave Jon Ossoff went low on Natalie Harp. analysis.brief_en: Western Australia is facing a potential 'black swan moment' as bird flu, specifically the H5N1 variant, threatens its flagship species, the black swan. The black swan, which serves as the state's bird emblem, is considered an indicator species for H5N1 due to its high visibility and low survival rates when infected. Experts warn of 'significant mortality' if the virus spreads to black swans, as they are ranked as 'very high risk' of infection. The WA government is testing a vaccine in five endangered black cockatoos at Perth zoo, produced by Zoetis, originally designed for chickens. However, the vaccine is not registered for use in wildlife and requires assessment before being used on native birds. The government has spent $113m on bird flu preparedness, but the effectiveness of the vaccine in native species remains uncertain. The virus has already caused three mass mortality events in South Australia involving over 1,000 greater crested terns, highlighting the potential for widespread impact on native bird populations. The black swan holds cultural and totemic significance for the Noongar people, adding to the emotional and ecological stakes of the situation.

news.title_zh: “毁灭性”:禽流感威胁旗舰物种,西澳大利亚州担心黑天鹅时刻 - 《卫报》
news.source_body_en: Western Australia is facing a potential 'black swan moment' as bird flu, specifically the H5N1 variant, threatens its flagship species, the black swan. The black swan, which serves as the state's bird emblem, is considered an indicator species for H5N1 due to its high visibility and low survival rates when infected. Experts warn of 'significant mortality' if the virus spreads to black swans, as they are ranked as 'very high risk' of infection. The WA government is testing a vaccine in five endangered black cockatoos at Perth zoo, produced by Zoetis, originally designed for chickens. However, the vaccine is not registered for use in wildlife and requires assessment before being used on native birds. The government has spent $113m on bird flu preparedness, but the effectiveness of the vaccine in native species remains uncertain. The virus has already caused three mass mortality events in South Australia involving over 1,000 greater crested terns, highlighting the potential for widespread impact on native bird populations. The black swan holds cultural and totemic significance for the Noongar people, adding to the emotional and ecological stakes of the situation.

AgriNerds to Create First-of-its-Kind, Dynamic Avian Influenza Surveillance System for U.S. Poultry Farmers News provided by Alveo Technologies Aug 25, 2026, 09:02 ET Share this article Share toX Share this article Share toX Linking on-site, rapid molecular HPAI testing to real-time HPAI modeling of migratory birds to help farmers run dynamic, risk-informed surveillance programs ALAMEDA, Calif., Aug. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Alveo Technologies, Inc., a global leader in rapid, point-of-need molecular diagnostics for early disease detection, today announced a strategic partnership with AgriNerds Inc, which has developed the Waterfowl Alert Network, a first-of-its-kind dynamic surveillance and awareness program that predicts historic and daily waterfowl activity around the nation's poultry and livestock farms. The partnership will pair Alveo's unique, rapid, molecular diagnostic with AgriNerds' Waterfowl Alert Network, a proprietary system that uses a combination of satellite imagery, weather radar, and telemetry to create daily farm-level HPAI risk scores based on remote sensing and HPAI surveillance data. To defend against HPAI and other pathogens, poultry producers have heavily invested in strengthening their biosecurity programs, but farms continue to suffer from HPAI outbreaks triggered by migratory birds, which is the source of infection for 68% of US H5N1 outbreaks since 2022, according to the APHIS. Currently, producers typically take one of two strategies for testing. Most test only when animals display flu-like symptoms, but this approach risks detecting the virus too late to prevent it from spreading. Some conduct periodic blind surveillance testing, which has the advantage of enabling early detection, but can be expensive. Alveo and AgriNerds are partnering to develop a new rapid and targeted approach: dynamic surveillance that alerts farmers when the risk of infection is high. AgriNerds' Waterfowl Alert Network will use radar imagery to detect migratory bird movements, analyze the data using AI-powered pattern recognition software, and generate daily risk scores it shares with customers. When risk escalates, Alveo's on-farm molecular test will help farms to conduct asymptomatic surveillance testing that provides precise results in under an hour, as opposed to waiting days for traditional PCR results to arrive from a lab. This targeted, risk-based testing approach is designed to lower costs and increase effectiveness, so farmers can detect the virus early and reduce its spread. "To stop the spread of HPAI, producers need tools that will enable them to monitor risk and, when it's elevated, employ rapid, accurate tests so they can take quick action and prevent further infection," said Shaun Holt, CEO of Alveo Technologies "This dynamic solution will aggregate and simplify rich data from AgriNerds' and deliver sophisticated risk assessments to users phones in a simple red, yellow and green format. They can then run surveillance tests based on informed risk and rapidly respond if bird flu is detected." The two organizations will use this feedback loop to strengthen the accuracy of risk assessments over time. As positive and negative test data accumulate across regions and seasons, both the risk alerts and testing guidance will become increasingly precise and valuable, securing the nation's food supply as well as producers' businesses. "Biosecurity extends far beyond the facility's fence line," said Maurice Pitesky, professor at UC Davis and CEO and co-founder of AgriNerds. "Our Waterfowl Alert Network gives farmers visibility into the dynamic risk landscape around their operations. When paired with Alveo's testing capability and rapid results, farmers can respond to real risks in real time. In this way, agriculture can move past reactive disease management to adopt a proactive, risk-informed approach." About AgriNerds: AgriNerds' veterinarians, epidemiologists, engineers, and waterfowl biologists are leveraging and repurposing various remote sensing-based technologies and applying modern statistical methods to help farmers usher in practical "off-site" risk assessments and HPAI risk predictions. The WaterFowl Alert Network is used by over 1,500 farms across 25 states and has the capacity to make historic and daily risk predictions for the entire U.S. poultry and livestock industry at the farm level. For more information, visit www.agrinerds.com. About Alveo Technologies: Alveo Technologies is a molecular diagnostics company that has developed a portable, cloud-connected platform that brings laboratory-quality pathogen detection directly to the Point of NeedTM for farmers, veterinarians and public health officials. By decentralizing molecular diagnostics, Alveo enables rapid detection and decision-making to help protect animal and human health, food security and supply chain resiliency. Alveo Sense Poultry provides avian influenza detection in approximately one hour, with results delivered through the Alveo Sense app. The Alveo platform incorporates machine learning technology to analyze assay data and provide automated interpretation of test results. Its growing portfolio includes molecular tests for avian influenza and other high-consequence pathogens. To learn more, visit alveotechnologies.com or follow us on LinkedIn. Product Availability Disclaimer: Product availability may vary by country or jurisdiction and is subject to applicable regulatory requirements and approvals. For information regarding availability in your country or jurisdiction, please contact Alveo Technologies at support@alveotechnologies.com. analysis.brief_en: Alveo Technologies and AgriNerds have partnered to create a dynamic avian influenza surveillance system for U.S. poultry farmers. This system combines rapid molecular testing with real-time modeling of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) based on migratory bird data. The initiative aims to provide farmers with precise results within an hour, significantly faster than traditional PCR testing, which can take days. The platform uses machine learning to interpret test results automatically, enhancing efficiency in risk management. This collaboration is designed to support farms in running proactive surveillance programs, reducing the impact of HPAI outbreaks. The system is currently being implemented and is intended to improve the ability of poultry farmers to respond to potential threats in a timely manner.

news.source_body_en: Alveo Technologies and AgriNerds have partnered to create a dynamic avian influenza surveillance system for U.S. poultry farmers. This system combines rapid molecular testing with real-time modeling of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) based on migratory bird data. The initiative aims to provide farmers with precise results within an hour, significantly faster than traditional PCR testing, which can take days. The platform uses machine learning to interpret test results automatically, enhancing efficiency in risk management. This collaboration is designed to support farms in running proactive surveillance programs, reducing the impact of HPAI outbreaks. The system is currently being implemented and is intended to improve the ability of poultry farmers to respond to potential threats in a timely manner.

news.content_title: Australia to evacuate scientists from sub-Antarctic island over bird flu risk
news.content: Australia to evacuate scientists from sub-Antarctic island over bird flu risk-Xinhua Australia to evacuate scientists from sub-Antarctic island over bird flu risk Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-08-28 10:59:45 CANBERRA, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- The Australian government said on Friday it will evacuate scientists from a sub-Antarctic island due to the "psychosocial risk" of a potential H5N1 avian influenza outbreak. The Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW) said it would temporarily withdraw staff from the Australian Antarctic Program's research station on Macquarie Island, a remote Australian territory located about 2,000 km southeast of the mainland. The DCCEEW said that the highly pathogenic H5N1 strain of bird flu has not been detected on the island, but that experts predict a high likelihood of significant mortality events during the upcoming breeding season. The island, which was added to UNESCO's World Heritage List for its outstanding universal value in 1997, is inhabited by up to 100,000 seals and millions of seabirds, including over 850,000 breeding pairs of endemic royal penguins, at various times throughout the year. "This is an unusual measure, but it's the most appropriate course of action based on our assessments of risk and operational realities," DCCEEW Deputy Secretary Sean Sullivan said in a statement. "While the risk to humans of H5 bird flu is considered low, we can't ignore the psychosocial risks of living near potentially large numbers of affected animals." The department said that the Australian Antarctic Program's flagship research and supply vessel, the RSV Nuyina, will travel to the island in late September or early October to retrieve 24 scientists, tradespeople and support staff as well as essential cargo. Options to monitor the situation on the island are under consideration and Sullivan said Australia remains committed to maintaining a long-term presence on Macquarie Island. ■ Australia to evacuate scientists from sub-Antarctic island over bird flu risk

news.content_title: Backyard Bird Feeders Drive H5N1 Spread After First Australian Mainland Mammal Death
news.content: A rainbow lorikeet eats from a tree on a spring morning along the Sydney Harbour on November 2, 2024. (Photo by SAEED KHAN / AFP) SAEED KHAN/AFP via Getty Images Australia confirmed on August 23 that a long-nosed fur seal found dead near the coastal town of Beachport had tested positive for H5N1 bird flu , making it the first mammal killed by the virus on mainland Australian soil. The announcement came as researchers published an urgent warning: the 50% of Australian households that routinely feed wild birds in their backyards are now inadvertently creating disease transmission hotspots that could accelerate the outbreak into species and places the virus has not yet reached. Fur Seal Death Brings H5N1 to Australian Mainland Mammals The long-nosed fur seal was discovered on August 19 at Beachport, a coastal town approximately 310 kilometers south of Adelaide in South Australia. Testing at CSIRO's Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness confirmed the diagnosis. South Australia's Chief Veterinary Officer, Skye Fruean, explained why seals were always at elevated risk: they share rocky coastal outcrops with wild birds already carrying the virus at high concentrations. "They would be coming across, no doubt, really high levels of the virus in their environment," Fruean said in televised remarks . Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins confirmed the case, offering an assessment that left no ambiguity about what comes next. "Once the H5 bird flu is spreading in the natural environment it is not possible to avoid significant losses," Collins told reporters . There is, as of August 24, no evidence the seal's death is part of a broader marine mammal outbreak — but researchers and conservation advocates were quick to emphasize that Australia should anticipate one . The fur seal death is the latest step in a rapid escalation. Australia confirmed its first mainland H5N1 case on June 19, 2026 — in a migratory brown skua at Cape Le Grand National Park in Western Australia. By August 22, the federal government had confirmed 297 cases nationwide . The outbreak has already killed more than 1,000 greater crested terns in South Australia and more than two dozen little penguins in Tasmania. A silver gull confirmed H5N1-positive at Robe in early August signaled that the virus had crossed from coastal seabirds into a species capable of traveling far inland — carrying the pathogen toward agricultural zones and urban environments that have so far remained unaffected. What Your Bird Feeder Is Actually Doing Against that backdrop, Darryl Jones — Professor Emeritus at Griffith University's Centre for Planetary Health and Food Security and the author of Feeding the Birds at Your Table: A Guide for Australia — published an expert analysis on August 24 explaining specifically why backyard bird feeders are now a problem. The mechanism is not mysterious. When a feeder is stocked, it draws birds of multiple species together at a density and in combinations that would never occur naturally. An infected silver gull, a healthy rainbow lorikeet, and a scavenging magpie do not share the same perch in the wild. At a suburban feeder, cross-species mixing becomes routine . "Feeding wild birds heightens the risk of disease transmission at feeding locations. When we offer supplementary food, such as seeds or meat scraps, this attracts birds of many different species in a combination and number that would not happen in nature. They may carry deadly diseases, such as the H5N1 virus, and potentially spread them to other birds. This can create a transmission hotspot right on deck ," Jones wrote. The epidemiological logic is well-established. Deakin University epidemiologist Marcel Klaassen provided the mechanistic explanation: "Infectious diseases like influenza spread through direct and indirect contact. If you create hotspots where birds aggregate and increase contact rates — for example through bird feeders — you increase that risk," Klaassen told the Biodiversity Council . Research synthesizing more than 20 studies of supplementary wildlife feeding and infectious disease found that intentional bird feeders consistently increase bacterial and viral pathogen transmission. The mechanism is straightforward: birds become more sedentary around a food source, accumulate at higher densities than natural foraging would produce, and leave behind a contaminated surface that multiple individuals visit repeatedly across the day. How Widespread Is the Risk? Research cited by Jones has found that approximately half of Australian households feed wild birds, with many doing so daily. That figure means the behavioral change being requested — stop feeding, or at minimum change how you feed — affects roughly five to six million Australian homes. Jones's own prior research offers something the public health message needs: evidence that stopping won't hurt the birds. Millions of Australians wake each morning and scatter seed on their back decks, watching birds arrive and taking pleasure in the ritual.
